headline: Park Avenue Gets Its Park Back—Plus Protected Bike Lanes
meta_description: NYC is transforming 11 blocks of Park Avenue with trees, seating, and a protected bike lane, restoring what was lost over a century ago.
summary_short: New York City is reclaiming Park Avenue's original character by adding green space and a two-way protected bike lane across 11 blocks, listening to community calls for s…
body:
New York City is reclaiming a piece of its own history. Park Avenue, which once literally contained a park running through its center until the 1920s, is being reimagined as a people-centered corridor stretching 11 blocks from 46th to 57th Street in Manhattan. The project converts one travel lane in each direction into a two-way protected bike lane, expands the median into vibrant public space with seating, plantings, and crosswalks, and brings back the trees and greenery that defined the avenue a century ago. The transformation reflects what Mayor Mamdani calls listening to New Yorkers: "This final design converts underused median space into vibrant public space while incorporating a dedicated, world-class bike connection."

The timing is strategic, born from necessity meeting opportunity. The avenue sits directly above Grand Central Terminal's train shed, which Metro-North Railroad is currently undergoing major capital rehabilitation to replace and waterproof. Rather than treating the avenue and the infrastructure below as separate projects, the city is coordinating them—aligning investment in modernizing aging infrastructure with a broader vision for public space shaped by community input. As transportation becomes cleaner and more active, the protected bike lane addresses a real safety concern for the growing number of New Yorkers who cycle or walk. NYC DOT Commissioner Mike Flynn framed it as foundational: the design "lays the foundation for future bike network upgrades in East Midtown."

What makes this story genuine is that it isn't about imposing a vision from above. It's about a city asking its residents what they need—more green, safer cycling—and then actually building it, even when it means removing car lanes. That's the harder choice, and it's the one they're making.
quick_facts: 11 blocks of Park Avenue being transformed, from 46th to 57th Street
One southbound vehicle lane converted into two-way protected bike lane
Park Avenue originally had a park running through it until the 1920s
Project coordinated with Grand Central Terminal train shed reconstruction
Expanded medians will feature seating, plantings, and public art
